before: I was about five when my mom told me it was time for bed (or something equally outrageous to a five-year-old). I cried and screamed "I HATE YOU!" She answered, "But I love you!"
after: When it's your little one yelling at you, try not to turn "But I love you" into a line you say on cue, because then it can brush the anger off, and what it's really saying is "so stop being angry." I think you can mean it and still be doing that. Does the love stay afterward, and hear the anger, and take whatever's true in it seriously?
brief:
- Joel's own reflection on that moment, in his first person

- her answer went against the feeling of the moment, and that may be exactly why it got through to him

- she added a second thing that was also true: his hating her didn't decide whether she loved him. He could hate somebody who loved him
- the relationship didn't have to match what he felt right then to still be real
- the guide's version tells it as "She did not tell me X. She introduced a second truth: Y" and ends on the lesson about the relationship. Don't copy those two moves

guide_passage: That completely threw me. Her answer did argue with the emotional logic of the moment, and that may be exactly why it reached me. She did not tell me I wasn’t angry. She introduced a second truth: my hatred did not determine her love. I could hate somebody who loved me. The relationship did not have to mirror my current emotion to remain real.
next: Don’t turn the sentence into a formula. “But I love you” can become dismissive when it means, “Therefore stop being angry.” The useful test is whether the love can remain alive, hear the anger, and take whatever is true in it seriously. Non-retaliation is one expression of love; it is not a colder substitute for love.
